title: Bertha Benz's long-distance drive
why_famous: The first long-distance automobile journey demonstrated that the motorcar could be practical transport.
route_summary: Mannheim to Pforzheim via Heidelberg, Wiesloch and Bruchsal; a different return through Bretten.
source_title: Mercedes-Benz: Bertha Benz and the long-distance journey
geometry_note: Town-level outward and return reconstruction. Connecting lines do not claim the exact unpaved road alignment of 1888.

title: First U.S. cross-country automobile drive
why_famous: Jackson, Crocker and their dog Bud completed the first automobile crossing of the United States.
route_summary: San Francisco to New York through the northern Rockies and Midwest.
source_title: Smithsonian: Crossing the Country
geometry_note: Chronological stop corridor, not a trace of individual roads or detours; no transcontinental highway existed.

title: Peking–Paris Motor Race
why_famous: Borghese's Itala crossed Asia and Europe, proving that automobiles could survive an unprecedented continental journey.
route_summary: Beijing through Mongolia and Siberia to European Russia, Germany and Paris.
source_title: Louwman Museum: The Peking–Paris Automobile Race in 1907
geometry_note: Borghese-focused named-place corridor; Gobi tracks and period roads are not surveyed geometry.

title: New York–Paris Race
why_famous: Schuster's Thomas Flyer won the intercontinental endurance contest through North America, Asia and Europe.
route_summary: New York to San Francisco by road, sea transfer to Valdez and back to Seattle, then via Japan to Vladivostok by ship; across Eurasia by road to Paris.
source_title: The Henry Ford: 1908 New York to Paris Race
geometry_note: Separate road and ship corridors. The American team landed in Alaska but did not drive across the Bering Strait; the Siberian roads remain generalized.

title: Stirling Moss's 1955 Mille Miglia
why_famous: Moss and Jenkinson's record-setting 300 SLR run became one of road racing's defining performances.
route_summary: The 1955 clockwise Brescia–Adriatic coast–Rome–Tuscany–Bologna–Brescia course.
source_title: 1000 Miglia: race history
geometry_note: 1955 route control points, with no claim that straight interpolations follow period pavement. Unlike revival routes, this follows the 1955 edition's broad loop.

title: First Paris–Dakar Rally
why_famous: Thierry Sabine's first desert rally launched the Dakar tradition.
route_summary: Paris to Marseille, Mediterranean transfer to Algiers, then the documented 1979 stage towns through Algeria, Niger, Mali and Senegal to Dakar.
source_title: Dakar Rally historical archive
geometry_note: Stage towns are more specific than the desert tracks. Actual paths between them and participant deviations remain unresolved.

anchors.name: Marseille
anchors.note: Ferry embarkation at Marseille; dock position approximated

title: First Baja 1000
why_famous: The first sanctioned Mexican 1000 established Baja's iconic desert endurance race.
route_summary: Tijuana and Ensenada south along Baja California to La Paz.
source_title: SCORE International: First Baja 1000
geometry_note: 1967 peninsula control corridor, not today's Baja 1000 course or exact desert trails.

title: First Carrera Panamericana
why_famous: The border-to-border race celebrated Mexico's Pan-American Highway and became an extreme road-racing test.
route_summary: Ciudad Juárez south through Chihuahua, Durango, Mexico City and Oaxaca to the Guatemala frontier.
source_title: La Carrera Panamericana: History
geometry_note: 1950 stage-city corridor. Straight links should not be read as the historical Pan-American Highway road centerline.

title: Alice Huyler Ramsey's cross-country drive
why_famous: Ramsey became the first woman to drive an automobile coast to coast in the United States.
route_summary: New York to San Francisco via the Midwest, Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada.
source_title: Smithsonian: Crossing the Country
geometry_note: Named-city reconstruction; individual farm roads, bridges and detours remain unverified.

title: London–Brighton Emancipation Run
why_famous: The celebratory motor run marked the relaxation of Britain's restrictive motoring rules.
route_summary: London to Brighton through Surrey and Sussex, including Reigate and Crawley corridors.
source_title: Motor Car Club's original 1896 route instructions (Royal Automobile Club archive)
geometry_note: The original 1896 instructions name Croydon, Reigate, Crawley and other intermediate places. These anchors follow that itinerary; individual road curves and vehicle positions remain approximate.
wiki_title: London to Brighton Veteran Car Run

title: Paris–Rouen motor competition
why_famous: The Paris–Rouen trial is widely considered the first organized automobile contest.
route_summary: Porte Maillot through Saint-Germain-en-Laye, Triel, Meulan, Mantes, Vernon, Gaillon and Pont-de-l'Arche to Rouen.
source_title: Pierre Giffard's account of the 1894 Paris–Rouen contest (1907)
geometry_note: The event organizer's published course identifies the mapped towns in order. City points approximate the historic road corridor; the individual road alignment and vehicle positions are not traced.

title: Paris–Bordeaux–Paris race
why_famous: The endurance event helped establish long-distance motor racing and the Automobile Club de France.
route_summary: Paris via Versailles, Étampes, Orléans, Blois, Tours, Poitiers and Angoulême to Bordeaux; return represented along the reciprocal official course.
source_title: La Locomotion Automobile: official Paris–Bordeaux–Paris course charts (1895)
geometry_note: The outbound anchors are named on the four contemporary official course plates. The return is drawn along that course in reverse; no individual competitor's wheel tracks are asserted, and modern street alignments are not reconstructed.

title: First French Grand Prix
why_famous: The inaugural Grand Prix established a demanding long public-road circuit near Le Mans.
route_summary: One 103-km 1906 Sarthe circuit lap, repeated six times on each of two days.
source_title: Automobile Club de l'Ouest: 1906 Grand Prix route
geometry_note: Period town and bend anchors describe one 1906 loop; temporary wooden bypasses at Saint-Calais and Vibraye are schematic, and repeated laps are metadata only.

title: First Targa Florio
why_famous: The race inaugurated one of motorsport's oldest and most difficult mountain-road contests.
route_summary: One Grande Circuito delle Madonie loop from Campofelice through Cerda, Petralia and Castelbuono, repeated three times.
source_title: Targapedia: 1906 first Targa Florio
geometry_note: The 1906 Grande circuit is represented by town anchors, not a later 72-km Piccolo loop or a claim of surveyed historic pavement.

title: First Indianapolis 500
why_famous: Ray Harroun won the first Indianapolis 500, one of the world's defining motor races.
route_summary: One counterclockwise 1911 Indianapolis Motor Speedway oval lap, repeated 200 times.
source_title: Indianapolis Motor Speedway: The first 500
geometry_note: Schematic four-corner 1911 oval footprint; race distance is 200 laps, not the single rendered loop. Exact banking and track edges are not traced.

title: Golden Flier suffrage tour
why_famous: Nell Richardson and Alice Burke carried the women's suffrage campaign to towns across the United States by automobile.
route_summary: New York to New Orleans, Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Minneapolis, Chicago, Detroit and back to New York.
source_title: Smithsonian: Traveling for Suffrage, Part 1
geometry_note: Only Smithsonian-listed principal stops are mapped, in reported order. The connectors are broad regional corridors, not the actual roads traveled.
wiki_title: Women's suffrage in the United States

title: First Pikes Peak Auto Hill Climb
why_famous: The inaugural Race to the Clouds began the famous ascent to Pikes Peak's summit.
route_summary: Original Crystal Reservoir start up the Pikes Peak Highway to the summit.
source_title: Pikes Peak International Hill Climb history
geometry_note: 1916 starting region differs from today's route. The anchors follow named highway landmarks, with modern coordinates used only for landmark position.

title: First 24 Hours of Le Mans
why_famous: The inaugural 24 Hours of Le Mans began the world's best-known endurance race.
route_summary: One 17.262-km 1923 Sarthe public-road circuit lap, repeated during 24 hours.
source_title: Automobile Club de l'Ouest: Origin of the 24 Hours
geometry_note: A 1923-specific schematic through Pontlieue, Tertre Rouge, Mulsanne, Arnage and Maison Blanche; current Le Mans barriers and chicanes are excluded.

title: First Mille Miglia
why_famous: The first Brescia–Rome–Brescia race established Italy's thousand-mile public-road classic.
route_summary: 1927 anticlockwise circuit via Parma, Bologna, Florence, Siena and Rome, returning via Umbria, the Adriatic, Treviso and Verona.
source_title: 1000 Miglia: The first race in 1927
geometry_note: Edition-specific town sequence differs substantially from 1955 and modern revival routes; straight links are not historical road centerlines.

title: First Monaco Grand Prix
why_famous: The first Monaco Grand Prix turned the principality's city streets into a motor-racing icon.
route_summary: One 1929 Boulevard Albert I–Casino–Station–Portier–harbour–Gasometer loop, repeated 100 times.
source_title: Automobile Club de Monaco: Club history
geometry_note: Historic corner sequence with approximate coordinates. The 1929 Station Hairpin, tunnel and Gasometer differ from later roadworks and today's circuit.

title: Ford's first Le Mans win
why_famous: Ford's GT40 victory ended Ferrari's run and produced a famous staged finish.
route_summary: One lap of the 1966, approximately 13.6-km Sarthe circuit, repeated through 24 hours.
source_title: Automobile Club de l'Ouest: Le Mans 66 archive
geometry_note: 1966 period circuit schematic, avoiding post-1990 Mulsanne chicanes and later infield sections. One loop shown; race mileage depends on laps.

title: London–Sydney Marathon
why_famous: The marathon rally took its competitors from London across Eurasia and Australia in a landmark endurance event.
route_summary: London to Bombay by road with a Dover–Calais ferry; Bombay to Fremantle by ship; Fremantle to Sydney by road.
source_title: British Motor Museum: 1968 London–Sydney Marathon
geometry_note: Control-city geometry follows the 1968 event; some crews chose different roads between controls. The two sea transfers are distinct from driving segments.

title: London–Mexico World Cup Rally
why_famous: Mikkola and Palm won a six-week rally linking Europe and the Americas in a Ford Escort.
route_summary: London to Lisbon by road, ship to Rio de Janeiro, drive through South America, ship across the Darién gap, then Central America to Mexico City.
source_title: Historic Marathon Rally Group: London to Mexico World Cup Rally
geometry_note: Documented control cities and sea transfers give the broad route. The Dover–Boulogne ferry is identified in a Ford rally retrospective; mountainous stage choices and ocean tracks remain unresolved.

additional_sources.note: Identifies the 1970 ferry crossing and interviews winning driver Hannu Mikkola.

title: First U.S. Army transcontinental motor convoy
why_famous: The Army's first coast-to-coast motor convoy tested whether heavy military vehicles could cross the United States; Dwight Eisenhower's experience later informed his support for improved national highways.
route_summary: Washington's Zero Milestone to Gettysburg, then the 1919 Lincoln Highway corridor through the Midwest, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada to Oakland; the convoy ferried across San Francisco Bay to its terminus.
source_title: Eisenhower Presidential Library — 1919 convoy daily log
geometry_note: Named towns and the final Oakland–San Francisco ferry come from the Army's day-by-day log. The line between them is a corridor, not a digitization of 1919 roadbeds; the convoy made local detours and the Lincoln Highway alignment changed over time.

additional_sources.title: Eisenhower Library expedition summary
additional_sources.note: Confirms dates, 3,251-mile scope and Eisenhower's participation.

title: 1903 Gordon Bennett Cup — Irish road circuit
why_famous: This international automobile race made the closed public-road circuit a model for early Grand Prix racing; Camille Jenatzy won for Germany in a Mercedes.
route_summary: The figure-eight Athy circuit combined an eastern loop through Castledermot and Carlow with a western loop through Kildare, Monasterevin, the Heath and Stradbally.
source_title: Into Kildare — historic Gordon Bennett route brochure
geometry_note: The two documented loops are drawn once each; the 1903 race repeated them (three eastern and four western laps). Town and control coordinates approximate the historic road course, not present-day driving directions. Ballyshannon is the Kildare crossroads, not the Donegal town.

additional_sources.title: Contemporary course map reproduced by motoring historians
additional_sources.note: Period route map shows the figure-eight control sequence.
